sentence: In many cases hernias cause no symptoms or very few.
The usual sign is a bulge or lump that may get bigger when the person coughs, sneezes or cries and smaller when they lie down.
Many hernias cause little or no pain.
Some hernias cause a visible lump, while others are internal, and in many cases there are no or very few symptoms.
A femoral hernia can also cause aching around the lump and discomfort when walking.
An umbilical hernia is usually painless, though in adults it can sometimes cause discomfort when coughing or straining.
Hiatus hernias typically cause heartburn, acid reflux, bloating, feeling sick, and difficulty or pain when swallowing.
These are also the symptoms of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
A hiatus hernia does not normally need treatment if it is not causing problems.
A hernia can form when muscle weakness lets tissue push through.
The NHS lists straining to poo, lifting heavy weights, being overweight, coughing, pregnancy and losing weight very quickly among possible causes.
MedlinePlus lists long-term constipation and straining, long-term coughing, extra weight, smoking and heavy exertion as contributors.
It also notes that inguinal hernias are more common in men.
Femoral hernias mainly happen in women over 50, but they can happen to anyone.
Being overweight appears on both the NHS and MedlinePlus lists.
For hiatus hernias, it is not exactly clear what causes them.
They may be due to the diaphragm weakening with age or pressure on the tummy.
Umbilical hernias are common in babies and often resolve on their own.
A GP can usually identify a hernia by examining the area.
The doctor may ask the person to stand, cough or strain while checking for a bulge.
Imaging such as ultrasound, CT or MRI is used when needed.
NIDDK says an inguinal hernia is diagnosed from the history and an examination of a lump in the groin.
For a hiatus hernia, if stronger medicines do not work, a GP can send the person for tests.
The NHS says to see a GP if a hiatus hernia causes symptoms that do not go away or pharmacy medicines do not help.
For an umbilical hernia, the NHS advises seeing a GP if the lump is painful, hard, does not move, or is growing or not going away.
The treatment offered depends on the type of hernia, what caused it, and whether it is new or has come back.
If a hernia causes only a noticeable lump with no pain or discomfort, it is reasonable to keep an eye on it without planning an operation.
NIDDK says men whose inguinal hernias cause few or no symptoms may be able to delay surgery, but should watch for symptoms and see a doctor regularly.
It also says most people with inguinal hernias will need surgery to repair them.
MedlinePlus adds that surgery is the only treatment that can permanently fix a hernia.
For adults with an umbilical hernia, the NHS says surgery is recommended for most because the hernia is unlikely to get better by itself and the risk of complications is higher.
Children usually do not need treatment for an umbilical hernia, which often disappears as they grow, though hospitals differ on timing.
note: Summary: children do not usually need treatment; trusts differ on timing.

sentence: A hiatus hernia is when part of the stomach moves up into the chest.
Symptoms can include heartburn, acid reflux, bloating and difficulty or pain when swallowing.
Most hiatus hernias need only lifestyle changes and medicines from a pharmacy.
Common advice includes eating smaller meals, raising the head of the bed, losing weight if overweight, stopping smoking, cutting back on alcohol and avoiding trigger foods.
Tight clothes around the waist are best avoided.
Pharmacists may recommend medicines called antacids or alginates, which can help ease symptoms.
Prescribed medicine should not be stopped without speaking to a doctor first.
Surgery is usually a last resort, when other treatments have not worked and very bad symptoms continue.
The main danger is strangulation, when the blood supply to trapped tissue is cut off.
This is a medical emergency, and a stuck or strangulated hernia needs emergency surgery.
note: NHS summary; NIDDK says emergency surgery.

sentence: Signs include a bulge that is suddenly larger or no longer goes back in, fever, redness, sudden or severe pain or tenderness, and bloating, nausea and vomiting.
The NHS femoral hernia page says to call 999 or go to A&E for very bad tummy pain, being sick, being unable to pass wind or stools, or a high temperature.
Strangulation of an umbilical hernia can lead to serious conditions such as sepsis and gangrene.
Hiatus hernia symptoms that need urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP the same day include weight loss without trying, difficulty swallowing, frequent vomiting, blood in vomit and upper tummy pain.
